title: 2 Kings 13:14–25
context: As Elisha lies dying, King Joash weeps over him. The prophet directs a sign with bow and arrows promising victory over Syria, but when the king strikes the ground only three times, Elisha says he will strike Syria only three times. Elisha dies, and a dead man thrown into his tomb revives on touching his bones. The chapter closes with the LORD’s covenant compassion toward Israel and Jehoash’s three victories over Benhadad. Both traditions read the passage as shared ground about God’s faithfulness to his word and the cost of incomplete trust.

verses.text: Now Elisha became sick with the illness of which he died; and Joash the king of Israel came down to him, and wept over him, and said, “My father, my father, the chariots of Israel and its horsemen!”
verses.arminianNotes:
Elisha falls sick with the illness from which he will die, and King Joash comes down to him, weeps, and cries, “My father, my father, the chariots of Israel and its horsemen!”

Arminian readers see a king honoring the prophet’s worth.
verses.reformedNotes:
The cry echoes Elisha’s own words at Elijah’s departure (2 Kings 2:12). The prophet, not the army, is called Israel’s true strength.

Reformed readers see the king recognizing that Israel’s security lay in the LORD’s word. Both traditions read this as clear shared ground.

verses.text: Elisha said to him, “Take bow and arrows;” and he took bow and arrows for himself.
verses.arminianNotes:
Elisha tells the king to take a bow and arrows, and he does so. The dying prophet begins a symbolic action.

Arminian readers see the king invited to participate actively in what God intends to do.
verses.reformedNotes:
Prophets in Israel sometimes acted out their messages, and this sign belongs to that pattern.

Reformed readers see God working through appointed means and signs. Both traditions read this as shared ground and describe the sign as the text presents it, without adding detail.

verses.text: He said to the king of Israel, “Put your hand on the bow;” and he put his hand on it. Elisha laid his hands on the king’s hands.
verses.arminianNotes:
Elisha tells the king to put his hand on the bow, and then lays his hands on the king’s hands. The gesture is personal and deliberate.

Arminian readers see the king’s action joined to the prophet’s blessing.
verses.reformedNotes:
The prophet’s hands on the king’s hands seem to signal that the coming victory depends on the LORD rather than the king’s strength alone.

Reformed readers see strength given from above. Both traditions read this as shared ground about victory coming from the LORD.

verses.text: He said, “Open the window eastward;” and he opened it. Then Elisha said, “Shoot!” and he shot. He said, “The LORD’s arrow of victory, even the arrow of victory over Syria; for you will strike the Syrians in Aphek until you have consumed them.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Elisha has the king open the east window and shoot, then declares the arrow the LORD’s arrow of victory over Syria, promising defeat of the Syrians at Aphek. The sign carries a promise.

Arminian readers see a real word of deliverance offered to Israel.
verses.reformedNotes:
Aphek had been the site of an earlier victory over Syria (1 Kings 20:26–30), though the exact location intended here is uncertain.

Reformed readers see God announcing his saving purpose. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the LORD’s promised victory.

verses.text: He said, “Take the arrows;” and he took them. He said to the king of Israel, “Strike the ground;” and he struck three times, and stopped.
verses.arminianNotes:
Elisha tells the king to take the arrows and strike the ground, and he strikes three times and stops. The king’s response is restrained.

Arminian readers see the king’s limited zeal as a genuine response with real effect on the outcome.
verses.reformedNotes:
The text does not state why Joash stopped. Readers often take it as half-heartedness, though that is an inference.

Reformed readers see the king’s response revealing his heart. Both traditions read this as shared ground about incomplete trust in the LORD’s promise.

verses.text: The man of God was angry with him, and said, “You should have struck five or six times. Then you would have struck Syria until you had consumed it, but now you will strike Syria just three times.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Elisha is angry and says Joash should have struck five or six times to consume Syria; now he will strike Syria only three times. The limited response yields limited victory.

Arminian readers see the outcome genuinely shaped by the king’s response.
verses.reformedNotes:
The prophet speaks of what would have followed a fuller response; counterfactual knowledge is treated at the box on 1 Samuel 23:12.

Reformed readers see God fulfilling his purpose through the king’s actual response. Both traditions read this as shared ground about incomplete trust.

verses.text: Elisha died, and they buried him. Now the bands of the Moabites invaded the land at the coming in of the year.
verses.arminianNotes:
Elisha dies and is buried, and Moabite raiding bands invade the land at the coming of the year. The narrative records the prophet’s death briefly.

Arminian readers see the end of a long and faithful ministry.
verses.reformedNotes:
‘The coming in of the year’ likely refers to spring, the usual season for campaigns, though the phrase is brief. Israel remains vulnerable.

Reformed readers see God’s servant finishing his course. Both traditions read this plainly as shared ground.

verses.text: As they were burying a man, behold, they saw a band of raiders; and they threw the man into Elisha’s tomb. As soon as the man touched Elisha’s bones, he revived, and stood up on his feet.
verses.arminianNotes:
While some are burying a man, they see a raiding band and throw the body into Elisha’s tomb; when the man touches Elisha’s bones, he revives and stands up. The text reports this plainly.

Arminian readers see the LORD’s power continuing after his servant’s death.
verses.reformedNotes:
The narrative gives no explanation beyond the event itself and draws no lesson about the bones.

Reformed readers see God confirming the prophet’s word even after his death. Both traditions read this as shared ground, describing the event as the text gives it.

verses.text: Hazael king of Syria oppressed Israel all the days of Jehoahaz.
verses.arminianNotes:
Hazael oppresses Israel all the days of Jehoahaz. The narrator returns to the political situation.

Arminian readers see the summary recalling the discipline described in verses 3–7, the consequence of Israel’s continued unfaithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse links the Elisha account back to the wider story of Syrian pressure on Israel.

Reformed readers see the backdrop against which God’s mercy in the next verse shines. Both traditions read this as shared ground about Israel’s long affliction under Syria.

verses.text: But the LORD was gracious to them, and had compassion on them, and favored them because of his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and would not destroy them and he didn’t cast them from his presence as yet.
verses.arminianNotes:
Yet the LORD is gracious and compassionate to Israel because of his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and does not yet destroy them or cast them from his presence. Mercy rests on covenant.

Arminian readers see real, responsive compassion (compare the box at Judges 10:16).
verses.reformedNotes:
‘As yet’ hints that judgment is delayed rather than canceled, anticipating 2 Kings 17.

Reformed readers see God’s covenant faithfulness preserving his people despite their sin. Both traditions read this as shared ground about God’s patience grounded in his promises.

verses.text: Hazael king of Syria died; and Benhadad his son reigned in his place.
verses.arminianNotes:
Hazael of Syria dies, and Benhadad his son reigns in his place. The balance of power begins to shift.

Arminian readers see the change preparing the way for the promised victories.
verses.reformedNotes:
The narrator simply notes the succession, which sets the stage for verse 25.

Reformed readers see God ordering the rise and fall of rulers for his purposes. Both traditions read this plainly as shared ground and do not go beyond the text in assessing Syria’s condition.

verses.text: Jehoash the son of Jehoahaz took again out of the hand of Benhadad the son of Hazael the cities which he had taken out of the hand of Jehoahaz his father by war. Joash struck him three times, and recovered the cities of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jehoash retakes from Benhadad the cities lost by his father, striking him three times and recovering Israel’s cities. The word of verse 19 is fulfilled.

Arminian readers see real deliverance, limited in scope by the king’s limited response.
verses.reformedNotes:
The number three ties the outcome to the arrow sign. The victories are genuine but partial.

Reformed readers see God’s word coming to pass exactly as spoken. Both traditions read this as shared ground about God’s faithfulness and the cost of incomplete trust.
